card.title: Relation Between Angular and Linear Velocity and Acceleration

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: The radius is the exchange rate between rotational and linear descriptions: $s = r\theta$, $v = r\omega$, $a_t = r\alpha$. Circular motion also carries a direction-changing acceleration $a_c = v^2/r = \omega^2 r$ toward the centre; the tangential part $r\alpha$ changes speed, and total acceleration is $\sqrt{a_c^2 + a_t^2}$.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - v = rω; a_t = rα - a_c = v²/r = ω²r = 4π²r/T² - a = √(a_c² + a_t²)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Rigid Body Constraint:** Relations like $v = r\omega$ and $a_t = r\alpha$ assume the particles are at a fixed distance $r$ from the axis of rotation (e.g., points on a rotating rigid body).  ·  **Instantaneous Values:** These relationships hold at any instant, even if $\omega$ or $\alpha$ are changing over time. They are local relations between linear and angular kinematics.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Angular velocity points ALONG THE AXIS (right-hand rule), not tangentially — this is the most common confusion.  ·  The kinematic equations for rotation are IDENTICAL in form to linear motion — just swap the variables.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: **Tangential vs centripetal:** $a_t = r\alpha$ changes speed; $a_c = v^2/r$ changes direction — uniform circular motion has only the second.  ·  **ω same for all points of a rigid body; v is not** — v scales with r.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Solve 5 problems converting between rpm, rad/s, and revolutions.  ·  Solve 5 problems using the kinematic equations for constant angular acceleration.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "Speed given → v²/r; rpm given → ω²r."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Numerical (3m): A particle moves in a circle of radius 2 m at 20 rad/s. Find its linear speed and centripetal acceleration.** — v = rω = 40 m/s; a_c = ω²r = 400 × 2 = 800 m/s², directed to the centre.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: The car-turn numerical repeats (2022, 2024) — memorise ω = v/r then a_c = v²/r.

rows.label: Classified table
rows.text: - Speeding up/slowing down: both components present. · Quantity | At rim (r large) | Near axis (r small) · $\omega$ | same | same · $v = r\omega$ | larger | smaller · $a_c = \omega^2 r$ | larger | smaller

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **Two forms of the same acceleration:** $a_c = v^2/r$ when speed is given, $a_c = \omega^2 r$ when rotation rate is given.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: $v = r\omega$; $a_t = r\alpha$; $a_c = v^2/r = \omega^2 r$; total $a = \sqrt{a_c^2 + a_t^2}$.  ·  Uniform circular motion: $a_t = 0$, acceleration is purely centripetal.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Centrifuges separate particles because a_c = ω²r grows with r and with the square of spin rate.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: A wheel rotates at 120 rpm. Its angular velocity in rad/s is: → B  ·  A disc starts from rest and accelerates at 2 rad/s². After 5 s, the angular displacement is: → B

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — One Motion, Two Languages The same rotating wheel can be described in radians per second or metres per second. The relations $s = r\theta$, $v = r\omega$, $a_t = r\alpha$ translate between the two languages — and they explain why outer rim points travel faster than inner ones on the same rigid body.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Derivation of $v = r\omega$ A particle on a circle of radius $r$ sweeps arc length $s = r\theta$. Differentiating with respect to time (r fixed): $$v = \frac{ds}{dt} = r\frac{d\theta}{dt} = r\omega$$ Differentiating again gives the **tangential acceleration** $a_t = r\alpha$ — the component that changes the *speed* along the circle.…  ·  ## 3. Worked Numericals **Q (3m, NEB-style):** A car takes a turn of radius 50 m at 10 m/s. Find the angular velocity and the centripetal acceleration. - $\omega = v/r = 10/50 = 0.2$ rad/s - $a_c = v^2/r = 100/50 = 2$ m/s² **Q (4m, NEB-style):** A flywheel starts from rest and reaches 300 rpm in 10 s.…

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Vector Interpretation:** These are scalar magnitudes of the cross-product relations $\vec{v} = \vec{\omega} \times \vec{r}$ and $\vec{a} = \vec{\alpha} \times \vec{r} + \vec{\omega} \times (\vec{\omega} \times \vec{r})$. The latter vector equation includes both tangential and centripetal terms.  ·  Always convert rpm to rad/s before using formulas — forgetting this is the most common calculation error.  ·  The number of revolutions is θ/(2π) — divide angular displacement in radians by 2π.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: NEB frequently asks: 'Find the number of revolutions' — use θ/(2π), not θ in radians.  ·  Note 1: Pay attention to the conditions under which Relation between angular and linear velocity and acceleration applies  ·  Note 2: Relation between angular and linear velocity and acceleration connects to multiple other topics in Science
